Compactness of the cube follows from [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and [[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]], and compactness of its image follows from [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. Preimages of Borel sets are Borel; disjoint preimages and countable additivity make the displayed set function a measure, and the box formula gives total mass one. The integral identity follows from indicators, increasing simple approximation and decomposition exactly as in one dimension. For translation invariance, discard the integer parts of the translation vector, split each coordinate of $[0,1)^n$ at its fractional part, and translate the resulting $2^n$ disjoint half-open boxes by integer vectors to partition the translated cube. The periodic preimage set is unchanged by these integer vectors; finite additivity and Lebesgue translation invariance give the same measure. Applying the indicator identity, simple approximation and decomposition gives the integral formula on any translated cube. The coordinate projections induce a continuous bijection
$\Phi:\mathbb T^n\to(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^n$ by the universal property. Its
domain is compact by the preceding check, while its codomain is a finite
product of Hausdorff spaces and hence Hausdorff ([[lem-products-preserve-t0-t1-and-hausdorff]]); the continuous-bijection
theorem therefore makes $\Phi$ a homeomorphism. Thus $\mathbb T^n$ carries the
finite product topology ([[def-product-topology]],
[[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]],
[[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), and its characters
$x\mapsto\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, are defined on this compact
Hausdorff space: replacing representatives by integer vectors leaves the exponential unchanged by [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and the trigonometric period. Finite products of the countable base above form a countable rectangular base. Hence every product-open set is a countable union of Borel rectangles. Conversely coordinate projections are continuous, so Borel rectangles are Borel in the product. Thus the product Borel sigma-algebra equals the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb T^n$. On a product $A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1}$ of Borel subsets
of the factors, the defining fundamental-domain formula and repeated application of [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] give
$m_{\mathbb T^n}(A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1})=\prod_jm_{\mathbb T}(A_j)$, so
$m_{\mathbb T^n}$ agrees on every measurable rectangle with the product measure
$m_{\mathbb T}\times\cdots\times m_{\mathbb T}$
([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]]); both are probability measures,
and uniqueness of the product measure on sigma-finite spaces identifies them
on the entire Borel sigma-algebra
([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).
Fubini's theorem then computes iterated integrals of $L^1$ functions on
$\mathbb T^n$
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

derivations.claim: Set $\sigma=\mu-\nu$, a complex measure by countable additivity. If its Fourier coefficients vanish, its integral against every trigonometric polynomial is zero. Given a continuous u, [F2] supplies polynomials arbitrarily close to u uniformly; [F1] bounds $|\int(u-p)d\sigma|$ by $\|u-p\|_\infty|\sigma|(\mathbb T)$. Therefore $\int u\,d\sigma=0$ for every continuous u.

For $z=r\zeta$, the geometric-series identity yields $$P(r\zeta,\eta)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}r^{|k|}\zeta^k\eta^{-k}.$$ At fixed r<1 this is uniformly absolutely convergent in both circle variables, with bound $1+2\sum_{k\ge1}r^k$. Integrating first against $\mu$ is justified by [F1] and the uniform error bound, and produces the uniformly convergent circle series $\sum_k r^{|k|}\widehat\mu(k)\zeta^k$, since $|\widehat\mu(k)|\le|\mu|(\mathbb T)$. Integrating this series against $\zeta^{-n}dm$ and using [F2] gives the stated coefficient formula.

Fix a Borel E and $\varepsilon>0$. Regularity in [F1] gives a compact $K\subseteq E$ and open $U\supseteq E$ with $|\sigma|(U\setminus K)<\varepsilon$. There is a continuous $0\le u\le1$ equal to one on K and zero outside U. Explicitly, if K is empty take u=0; if U is the circle take u=1; otherwise use $$u(x)=\frac{d(x,\mathbb T\setminus U)}{d(x,\mathbb T\setminus U)+d(x,K)}.$$ The two sets are disjoint closed sets, so the denominator is positive at each x; distances are continuous because $|d(x,A)-d(y,A)|\le d(x,y)$ for a nonempty set A. Thus $|\mathbf1_E-u|\le\mathbf1_{U\setminus K}$. Step 1.1 and [F1] give $|\sigma(E)|=|\int(\mathbf1_E-u)d\sigma|<\varepsilon$. Hence $\sigma(E)=0$ for every E, proving Fourier uniqueness.

If $P[\mu]=P[\nu]$, fix r=1/2 in step 1.2. Every factor $r^{|n|}$ is strictly positive, so all Fourier coefficients agree. Step 2.1 gives $\mu=\nu$. Zero measures and zero variation cause no division by a measure mass anywhere in the proof.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 handles K empty by the zero cutoff, and U equal to the full circle by the constant-one cutoff; the empty Borel E requires no distance to an empty set.
For two zero measures, step 1.1 has all coefficient integrals zero and every total-variation bound zero; step 3.1 proves equality without dividing by a measure mass.

The zero-index coefficient recovers the total mass, but all integer coefficients are required. In particular comparison with Haar measure, whose coefficients are one only at zero, is covered by steps 1.1–2.1.
Step 2.1 uses positive regular variation of the complex difference, so signed cancellation of masses is controlled; the compact/open cutoff proof is valid for complex measures.
Step 1.2 requires 0<r<1, and step 3.1 fixes r=1/2. The radius r=0 alone would not detect nonzero Fourier modes and is not used for uniqueness.

CC is explicit in Given and the finite-variation/trigonometric density suppliers of steps 1.1–2.1; each compact/open approximation is chosen for a fixed E and epsilon, without an arbitrary simultaneous family.

boundaries.reason: The Statement proves equality of measures from equal coefficients and equal Poisson integrals; it is not an iff characterization of arbitrary coefficient sequences.
The geometric-series coefficient identity in step 1.2 holds for supplied measures; no existence theorem for measures with arbitrary integer data is asserted.

risk_review.notes: Steps 1.1–3.1 checked: finite regular variation bounds uniform approximation, so zero Fourier moments imply zero integrals against all continuous data.
